activity-topic.answer: The activity or whole business of getting up early, treated as a topic.

abstract-superlative.rule: Lo más or lo menos plus an adjective forms an abstract extreme
abstract-superlative.example: ___ ___ importante es descansar. (The most important thing)

personal-obligation.rule: Tener que commonly states a personal requirement; deber often gives advice or moral duty
personal-obligation.example: Si quieres aprobar, ___ ___ estudiar. (If you want to pass, you have to study)

legacyAliases.rule: tener que = personal must (forced by circumstance); deber = moral should (it's the right thing)
legacyAliases.example: Si quieres aprobar, ___ ___ estudiar. (If you want to pass, you have to study)

conditional-advice.example: ___ llamarla. (You should call her; tú, softened advice with deber.)

probability-application.rule: Deber de marks inference; deber without de can also express probability
probability-application.example: Son las diez de la noche, Juan ___ ___ estar dormido. (It's 10 pm, Juan must be asleep — guessing)

legacyAliases.rule: deber + inf = should (advice); deber DE + inf = must be (probability)
legacyAliases.example: Son las diez de la noche, Juan ___ ___ estar dormido. (It's 10 pm, Juan must be asleep — guessing)

probability-without-de.rule: Absence of de does not force an obligation reading
probability-without-de.example: Must Debe estar en casa always mean an obligation rather than a guess?
probability-without-de.answer: No. Deber with or without de can express probability; context disambiguates the form without de.

impersonal-necessity.rule: Impersonal haber que stays third-person singular
impersonal-necessity.example: Antes ___ que ser puntual. (One had to be punctual; imperfect.)

haber-de-register.rule: Haber de has formal/literary associations but remains current in some regions
haber-de-register.example: Does He de irme sound equally neutral and frequent everywhere?
haber-de-register.answer: No. Haber de is often formal or literary, but remains conversationally current in some regions, including parts of Mexico and Spain.

possessive-form-families.rule: Mi, tu and su have distinct long forms
possessive-form-families.example: Which long possessive bases correspond to short mi, tu and su?
possessive-form-families.answer: Mío, tuyo and suyo, each agreeing in gender and number with the possessed noun.

unchanged-families.rule: Nuestro and vuestro use the same gender/number forms in both positions
unchanged-families.example: Which two possessive families do not need a distinct short-versus-long base?
unchanged-families.answer: Nuestro and vuestro, with their ordinary gender and number agreement.

possessed-noun-agreement.rule: Long-form possessives agree with the thing possessed (gender + number), not the owner
possessed-noun-agreement.example: María tiene un coche pequeño. Es un coche ___. (her car; add the long possessive)

legacyAliases.rule: Long-form possessives agree with the thing possessed (gender + number), not the owner
legacyAliases.example: María tiene un coche pequeño. Es ___ ___ (her car) ___. (Add long possessive after the noun)

female-friend.rule: Mía agrees with a feminine singular possessed noun

standalone-article.rule: As a standalone pronoun, the long possessive needs an article: el mío, la tuya, los suyos
standalone-article.example: Mi coche es viejo, pero ___ ___ es nuevo. (yours)

legacyAliases.rule: As a standalone pronoun, the long possessive needs an article: el mío, la tuya, los suyos
legacyAliases.example: Mi coche es viejo, pero ___ ___ (yours - el coche tuyo) es nuevo.

predicate-no-article.rule: A predicate possessive directly after ser normally omits the article

suyo-ambiguity.rule: Suyo does not identify a unique owner
suyo-ambiguity.example: Which owners can suyo refer to, and how can you explicitly specify a female third-person owner?
suyo-ambiguity.answer: His, hers, formal singular yours, plural yours or theirs; de ella explicitly identifies her.

stressed-a-feminine.rule: Uno, alguno and ninguno can shorten before feminine stressed-a nouns
stressed-a-feminine.example: Why can un águila, algún águila and ningún águila occur even though águila is feminine?
stressed-a-feminine.answer: Uno, alguno and ninguno also shorten before feminine nouns beginning with stressed a or ha; the noun remains feminine.

masculine-apocope.rule: bueno/malo/primero/tercero/alguno/ninguno/uno drop final -o before a masculine singular noun
masculine-apocope.example: No tengo ___ problema con eso. (I have no problem with that)

full-form-after.rule: Bueno keeps its full inflected form after a noun
full-form-after.example: Es un amigo ___. (good; put the adjective after the noun)

ordinal-third.rule: Tercero shortens before a masculine singular noun

intervening-modifier.rule: A modifier does not necessarily block apocopation in the noun phrase

gran-quality.rule: Grande normally shortens before singular nouns of either gender, often with a quality reading
gran-quality.example: Cervantes fue un ___ escritor. (Cervantes was a great writer)

legacyAliases.rule: grande → gran before any singular noun; meaning shifts (gran = great; grande after noun = physically big)
legacyAliases.example: Cervantes fue un ___ escritor. (Cervantes was a great writer)

gran-size-contrast.rule: Position often distinguishes greatness from physical size
gran-size-contrast.example: How does una gran ciudad usually differ from una ciudad grande?
gran-size-contrast.answer: The first praises a great city; the second describes a physically big city.

grande-comparative-exception.rule: Más or menos blocks the usual shortening of grande
grande-comparative-exception.example: Es la más ___ ciudad de la región. (big)

saint-name.rule: Most male saint names take san

saint-exception-cue.rule: Do-/To- recalls conventional Santo exceptions, not an unrestricted prefix rule
saint-exception-cue.example: Which Santo exceptions does the Do-/To- memory cue recall, and what is its limit?
saint-exception-cue.answer: Santo Domingo, Santo Tomás, Santo Tomé and Santo Toribio; the cue recalls these names rather than predicting every Do-/To- name.

hundred-noun.rule: One hundred is cien before a noun, mil or millones, and on its own

any-feminine.rule: Cualquiera shortens before a singular noun of either gender

cualesquiera-register.rule: Cualesquiera is a literary plural; cualquiera de selects one member
cualesquiera-register.example: What register does cualesquiera have, and how would you commonly say any one of the books?
cualesquiera-register.answer: It is rare or literary; cualquiera de los libros selects any one of the books.

gnomic-present.rule: Proverbs typically use gnomic present (indicative) for universal truths

gnomic-assertion.rule: Generic reference does not automatically require subjunctive
gnomic-assertion.example: Why do the relative clauses in these gnomic proverbs use indicative despite describing general situations?
gnomic-assertion.answer: The speaker presents the pattern as a timeless, factual truth, rather than a merely sought or hypothetical case.

affirmative-pronoun.rule: An object pronoun attaches to the affirmative tú command di
affirmative-pronoun.example: ___ con quién andas y te diré quién eres. (Tell me)

negative-command.rule: Negative tú commands use present subjunctive
negative-command.example: A caballo regalado no le ___ el diente. (mirar)

command-irregulars.rule: The regular third-person-present shortcut has irregular tú-command exceptions
command-irregulars.example: Do decir, hacer and salir form affirmative tú commands by copying dice, hace and sale?
command-irregulars.answer: No. Their commands are di, haz and sal.

hypothetical-concession.example: Aunque la mona ___ de seda, mona se queda. (vestirse)

legacyAliases.rule: 'Aunque' + subjunctive marks a hypothetical concession
legacyAliases.example: Aunque ___ la mona de seda, mona se queda. (vestir)

future-subjunctive-fossil.rule: Fueres and vieres preserve archaic future subjunctive
future-subjunctive-fossil.example: What mood and tense are fueres and vieres in the proverb, and what are their modern equivalents here?
future-subjunctive-fossil.answer: Future subjunctive; modern Spanish normally uses vayas and veas here.

nonexistence-relative.rule: A negated nonexistent antecedent takes subjunctive
nonexistence-relative.example: No hay mal que por bien no ___. (venir)

open-condition.rule: An open si condition uses present indicative before an imperative result
open-condition.example: Si ___ paz, prepárate para la guerra. (querer; tú)

counterfactual-result.rule: A present counterfactual pairs imperfect subjunctive with conditional
counterfactual-result.example: Si yo tuviera tu juventud, ___ el mundo. (conquistar)

better-than.rule: Más vale A que B expresses preference or greater worth

equality-comparison.rule: Tan plus adjective uses como for equality

adjective-comparison.rule: Más plus an adjective takes que for greater degree
adjective-comparison.example: Más rápido ___ un rayo. (Faster than lightning.)

er-ir-present-contrast.rule: Regular -er and -ir present endings differ in nosotros and vosotros
er-ir-present-contrast.example: Which two subject slots distinguish regular -er from -ir present endings?

same-form-context.rule: Some regular nosotros present and preterite forms coincide
same-form-context.example: Can hablamos and vivimos each be either present or preterite?
same-form-context.answer: Yes. Context distinguishes them; comemos and comimos do not have this ambiguity.

ar-present.example: Vosotros ___ español. (hablar; present, Spain informal plural)

ar-imperfect.rule: Imperfect -ar nosotros retains the stressed aba syllable

ar-future.rule: Regular future adds endings to the whole infinitive
ar-future.example: Mañana yo ___ con Ana. (hablar; simple future)

ar-conditional.rule: Regular conditional adds -ía to the infinitive for yo

ar-subjunctive.rule: Regular -ar present subjunctive uses e endings

er-subjunctive.rule: Regular -er present subjunctive uses a endings
er-subjunctive.example: Espero que vosotros ___ bien. (comer; Spain informal plural)

ir-preterite.example: Tú ___ en Madrid el año pasado. (vivir)

ir-future.rule: Regular -ir future also keeps the whole infinitive

ir-subjunctive.rule: Regular -ir present subjunctive uses the same a endings as -er

compound-present.rule: Compound tenses = conjugated haber + past participle (never changes)

compound-future.example: Yo ___ comido antes de las tres. (will have eaten)

compound-conditional.example: Yo ___ comido si hubiera tenido tiempo. (would have eaten)

compound-subjunctive.rule: Present perfect subjunctive uses present subjunctive haber

participle-invariance.rule: A participle after auxiliary haber does not agree with the subject
participle-invariance.example: Should the participle change for a feminine plural subject in Ellas han comido?
participle-invariance.answer: No. Keep comido; only the auxiliary agrees with the subject.

preterite-hacer.rule: Hacer changes preterite hic- to hiz- before o

preterite-decir.rule: Decir uses dij- and ellos -eron without i

preterite-ir-ser.rule: Ir and ser share a special preterite paradigm
preterite-ir-ser.example: Which preterite forms are shared by ir and ser, and how is the intended verb identified?
preterite-ir-ser.answer: Fui, fuiste, fue, fuimos, fuisteis, fueron; context identifies going versus being.

preterite-dar.rule: Dar has a special short preterite without written accents

future-tener.rule: Tener shares tendr- between future and conditional

future-salir.rule: Salir shares saldr- between future and conditional

future-poner.rule: Poner shares pondr- between future and conditional
future-poner.example: Mañana yo ___ la mesa. (poner; simple future)

future-venir.rule: Venir shares vendr- between future and conditional

future-haber.rule: Haber shares habr- between future and conditional
future-haber.example: Yo ___ terminado para entonces. (haber; future perfect)

future-poder.rule: Poder shares podr- between future and conditional

future-saber.rule: Saber shares sabr- between future and conditional
future-saber.example: Yo lo ___ si me lo dijeran. (saber; conditional)

future-querer.rule: Querer shares querr- between future and conditional

future-hacer.rule: Hacer shares har- between future and conditional

future-decir.rule: Decir shares dir- between future and conditional
future-decir.example: Mañana yo te lo ___. (decir; simple future)

stress-default-mnemonic.rule: The n/s/vowel cue recalls qualified default stress
stress-default-mnemonic.example: Recall the n/s/vowel stress shortcut, its syllable mapping, and the qualifications for consonant clusters and final y.
stress-default-mnemonic.answer: n, s, vowel → llana default; other consonants → aguda default. Llana means second-to-last stress; aguda means final stress. The n/s shortcut applies only when n or s is not preceded by another consonant; final y counts as a consonant.

llana-accent-condition.rule: Llanas take a tilde with other-consonant endings including clusters and final y
llana-accent-condition.example: When does a llana, stressed on the second-to-last syllable, need a tilde under the general rules?
llana-accent-condition.answer: When it ends in a consonant other than single n or s, including consonant + n/s and final y.

llana-arbol-application.rule: Words ending in vowel, n, or s are llanas by default — no tilde unless stress falls elsewhere
llana-arbol-application.example: The word 'árbol' carries a tilde because it ends in ___ and is stressed on the first syllable.
llana-arbol-application.answer: l (a consonant other than n or s)

aguda-accent-condition.rule: Agudas take a tilde with a vowel or single n/s ending
aguda-accent-condition.example: When does an aguda, stressed on the last syllable, need a written tilde?
aguda-accent-condition.answer: When it ends in a vowel, or in n or s not preceded by another consonant.

esdrujula-accent.example: A word is stressed on its third-to-last syllable. Does its final letter decide whether it takes a tilde?
esdrujula-accent.answer: No. Esdrújulas always take a tilde.

sobreesdrujula-application.rule: Verb-plus-pronoun sobresdrújulas keep a written stress mark
sobreesdrujula-application.example: Add the required tilde to digamelo (tell it to me), stressed on dí.

diacritic-memory-cue.rule: The lean-on cue recalls conventional stressed diacritic members, not arbitrary emphasis
diacritic-memory-cue.example: What does the lean-on mnemonic mean for diacritic pairs, and why is it not a universal accent rule?
diacritic-memory-cue.answer: It associates the stressed member with pronouns like tú, question words like qué and affirmation sí; stressed té and sé still require their learned meanings. Emphasis alone does not license a tilde.

interrogative-indirect.rule: Interrogative words retain their tilde inside indirect questions
interrogative-indirect.example: Does cómo lose its tilde in No sé cómo se escribe because there are no question marks?
interrogative-indirect.answer: No. It introduces an indirect question and keeps the tilde.

diacritic-tu-contrast.example: What is the difference between tu and tú?
diacritic-tu-contrast.answer: tu means your (possessive); tú means you (subject pronoun).

diacritic-el-application.rule: The subject pronoun él takes a tilde
diacritic-el-application.example: ___ me lo explicó ayer. (He explained it to me yesterday.)

hiatus-weak-vowel-condition.rule: A stressed i/u next to an unstressed a/e/o requires a tilde
hiatus-weak-vowel-condition.example: What happens when a stressed i or u is next to an unstressed a, e, or o?
hiatus-weak-vowel-condition.answer: They form a hiato, and the stressed i or u takes a tilde even if the general accent rules would not require one.

hiatus-pais-application.rule: País marks a stressed weak vowel in hiatus
hiatus-pais-application.example: Write the Spanish word for country with its required accent mark: pais.

diphthong-general-rules.rule: Diptongos still follow the general accent rules
diphthong-general-rules.example: Does having a diptongo mean a word can never carry a tilde? Use canción as a check.
diphthong-general-rules.answer: No. Diptongos follow the general accent rules; canción takes a tilde because it is aguda and ends in n.

two-strong-vowels.rule: Two strong vowels form hiatus without automatically requiring a tilde
two-strong-vowels.example: Do the adjacent vowels in caer form one syllable, and must a tilde be added just to separate them?
two-strong-vowels.answer: They form two syllables, ca-er; no extra tilde is needed solely for that hiatus.

two-weak-vowels.rule: Two different weak vowels count as a diphthong for general accentuation
two-weak-vowels.example: How are two different adjacent weak vowels, i and u, treated by the accentuation pattern described here?
two-weak-vowels.answer: As a diphthong following the general accent rules.

solo-ambiguity-qualification.rule: An optional tilde on adverbial solo is limited to possible ambiguity
solo-ambiguity-qualification.example: Under current RAE guidance, is sólo an unrestricted alternative whenever solo means only?
solo-ambiguity-qualification.answer: No. An optional tilde is limited to adverbial solo where the writer judges a risk of ambiguity; writing solo without a tilde is recommended.

demonstrative-ambiguity-qualification.rule: Demonstrative tildes are limited to potentially ambiguous pronoun uses
demonstrative-ambiguity-qualification.example: When may este, ese, or aquel optionally carry a tilde, and can esto ever take one?
demonstrative-ambiguity-qualification.answer: Only in pronominal uses with a risk of ambiguity; not when accompanying a noun. Esto, eso, and aquello never take a tilde.

enye-uppercase.rule: Ñ retains the distinguishing mark of ñ in capitals
enye-uppercase.example: Write España entirely in capital letters.

uppercase-accent-application.rule: Capitalization does not remove required accent marks
uppercase-accent-application.example: Write África entirely in capital letters, preserving correct spelling.

three-verb-cue.rule: Identity-condition-existence is a qualified three-way memory cue
three-verb-cue.example: Recall the three-part cue for choosing among Spanish verbs translated as be, including haber's second job.
three-verb-cue.answer: Ser = identity; estar = condition; haber = existence/auxiliary. Ser also locates events, estar locates things or people, and haber builds compound tenses.

ser-profession.rule: Ser states a profession without an article before the bare occupation

ser-clock.rule: Clock time uses singular es at one and plural son for other hours

ser-event.rule: Event location uses ser even for a temporary event

estar-known-location.rule: Estar locates a known person or thing

estar-state.rule: Estar presents a current physical or emotional state

estar-weather.rule: Nublado with estar describes current weather

estar-result.rule: A participle after estar describes a resulting or adjectival state and agrees

estar-calendar.rule: Estamos a introduces the current calendar date

haber-existence.rule: Ser = identity/essence; Estar = state/location; Haber (hay) = existence
haber-existence.example: ___ tres libros en la mesa. (There are three books on the table.)

haber-singular-past.rule: Existential haber remains singular in the past too

haber-weather.rule: Hay can introduce a weather noun

haber-obligation.rule: Impersonal hay que takes an infinitive

haber-auxiliary.rule: Auxiliary haber agrees with its subject in compound tenses

archaic-ha-time.rule: Elapsed-time ha is archaic or literary; common hace comes from hacer
archaic-ha-time.example: Are literary ha in años ha and everyday hace tres años forms of the same verb?
archaic-ha-time.answer: No. Ha is from haber; hace is from hacer. Elapsed-time ha is archaic or literary.

weirdo-mnemonic.rule: WEIRDO recalls six trigger categories, not an exhaustive automatic rule
weirdo-mnemonic.example: Expand WEIRDO, map each letter to a trigger category and example, and state what the mnemonic does not guarantee.
weirdo-mnemonic.answer: WEIRDO means an odd person. W = Wishes/volition (querer que); E = Emotions (alegrarse de que); I = Impersonal expressions (es posible que); R = Recommendations (recomendar que); D = Doubt/denial (dudar que); O = Ojalá (I hope/if only). It is a memory cue, not an exhaustive or exception-free rule.

ojala-application.rule: Ojalá takes subjunctive even without que
ojala-application.example: Ojalá ___ mañana. (llover; I hope it rains.)

wish-application.rule: A hope that someone comes takes present subjunctive

legacyAliases.rule: WEIRDO triggers (Wishes, Emotions, Impersonal expressions, Recommendations, Doubt, Ojalá) require the subjunctive in the subordinate clause
legacyAliases.example: Espero que tú ___ (venir) mañana.

same-subject-infinitive.rule: A neutral same-subject wish normally uses an infinitive
same-subject-infinitive.example: How does neutral I want to go differ structurally from I want you to come?
same-subject-infinitive.answer: Quiero ir uses an infinitive with the same subject; Quiero que vengas uses que plus subjunctive for the other subject.

command-versus-report.rule: Decir que changes mood according to command versus report
command-versus-report.example: How do Te digo que vengas and Te digo que viene differ?
command-versus-report.answer: The first tells you to come, a command with subjunctive; the second reports that someone is coming, with indicative.

factual-emotion.rule: An emotional reaction can take subjunctive about a known fact
factual-emotion.example: Does Me alegro de que estés aquí imply uncertainty about whether you are here?
factual-emotion.answer: No. The presence can be known; subjunctive marks the emotional reaction rather than asserting the fact anew.

emotion-application.rule: An emotional reaction uses subjunctive in its complement
emotion-application.example: Me alegro de que ___ aquí. (estar; tú)

impersonal-fact-exception.rule: Fact-asserting impersonal expressions take indicative rather than automatically following WEIRDO
impersonal-fact-exception.example: Why do Es posible que and Es seguro que normally select different moods?
impersonal-fact-exception.answer: Possibility takes subjunctive; certainty asserts a fact and takes indicative. Negating the assertion normally brings subjunctive.

purpose-clause.rule: Para que selects subjunctive in a finite purpose clause
purpose-clause.example: Te lo digo para que lo ___. (saber; tú)

known-past-before.rule: Antes de que selects subjunctive even for a known past sequence
known-past-before.example: Llegué antes de que ___. (empezar; it started)

future-cuando.rule: An anticipated future cuando clause uses present subjunctive
future-cuando.example: Cuando ___, comeremos. (llegar; he arrives in the future)

aunque-qualification.rule: Aunque plus subjunctive need not deny a known fact
aunque-qualification.example: Does subjunctive after aunque always prove that the concession is unknown or unreal?
aunque-qualification.answer: No. It can mark a hypothetical concession or background a known fact as conceded.

past-after-variation.rule: Past después de que has regional and register variation
past-after-variation.example: Is indicative the only possible mood after después de que for an event that really happened?
past-after-variation.answer: No. Indicative is common, but subjunctive also occurs with known past events, depending on variety and register.

mientras-meanings.rule: Mientras has temporal and conditional uses
mientras-meanings.example: How does mientras differ in Mientras estudiaba, llamó and Mientras estudies, te ayudo?
mientras-meanings.answer: The first means while, describing a past temporal overlap with indicative; the second means as long as, setting a condition with subjunctive.

unknown-antecedent.rule: A sought unknown antecedent takes subjunctive
unknown-antecedent.example: Busco un libro que ___ interesante. (ser; any book that fits, none identified)

nonexistent-antecedent.rule: Negated existence takes subjunctive in the relative clause
nonexistent-antecedent.example: No hay nadie que ___ la respuesta. (saber)

antecedent-memory-test.rule: Specific-X versus any-X is a meaning test, not an article test
antecedent-memory-test.example: How does the specific X versus any X that fits shortcut map to relative-clause mood?
antecedent-memory-test.answer: A specific known X points to indicative; an unknown, sought or nonexistent X points to subjunctive. The speaker's intended reference matters, not simply el versus un.

past-trigger.rule: A past desire normally pairs with imperfect subjunctive
past-trigger.example: Quería que ___ a la cena. (venir; tú, usual past sequence)

present-prior-action.rule: A present reaction to prior completed action can use perfect subjunctive
present-prior-action.example: Me alegra que ___ venido. (haber; tú, already happened)

past-prior-action.rule: Pluperfect subjunctive can mark action prior to a past trigger
past-prior-action.example: Había querido que ___ venido antes. (haber; tú, prior action)

sequence-qualification.rule: The usual subjunctive tense sequence is not an absolute prohibition
sequence-qualification.example: Does every past-tense main clause categorically ban present subjunctive in its complement?
sequence-qualification.answer: No. The chart gives the usual sequence; present relevance, regional usage and present-perfect main clauses can affect the choice.
